overview.title: Prediction output and chapter 3 summary
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.main_topic: The output of model.predict() on the linear model, followed by the end-of-chapter summary for chapter 3.
overview.central_idea: The trained linear model produces one scalar score per sample; with that, the Keras workflow (layers -> model -> compile -> fit -> predict) is complete, sitting on top of interchangeable low-level backends (TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX).
overview.importance: This page is the checkpoint between learning the tools (chapter 3) and applying them to real problems (chapter 4). The six bullets are the minimum mental model you need for everything that follows.
learning_objectives: Read and interpret the (10, 1) prediction array printed by predict().
Convert the linear model's scores into class decisions.
Recall the six summary points of chapter 3 and relate each to the section where it was taught.
Distinguish the roles of low-level frameworks and the high-level Keras API.
prerequisites: model.predict() and the linear model of Listing 3.35 (p.125-126)

summary:
The page opens with the output of `print(predictions[:10])` from p.126: a NumPy array of shape (10, 1) holding ten scalar scores, from `0.025846` to `0.82706255`. These are the raw outputs of the linear `Dense(1)` model of Listing 3.35, which was trained with mean squared error toward targets 0 and 1, so scores close to 1 point to one class and scores close to 0 to the other.

The authors then say that this is all you need to know about Keras models for now, and that chapter 4 moves on to real-world problems with Keras.

The chapter **Summary** has six bullets:

1. **TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX** are three popular low-level frameworks for numerical computation and autodifferentiation, each with its own way of doing things and its own strengths and weaknesses (sections 3.3-3.5).
2. **Keras** is a high-level API for building and training neural networks and runs on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX: pick the backend you like (section 3.6, p.115).
3. The central Keras class is **`Layer`**: a layer encapsulates weights and computation, and layers are assembled into models (sections 3.6.2-3.6.3).
4. Before training you choose an **optimizer, a loss and metrics** with `model.compile()` (sections 3.6.4-3.6.5).
5. **`fit()`** runs mini-batch gradient descent for you and can monitor loss and metrics on **validation data** the model does not train on (sections 3.6.6-3.6.7).
6. After training, **`model.predict()`** generates predictions on new inputs (section 3.6.8).

The summary leaves out `evaluate()`, which p.126 also covered.

paragraphs.excerpt: For now, this is all you need to know about Keras models.
paragraphs.what_it_says: This closes the Keras introduction: what has been covered is sufficient for now, and the next chapter applies Keras to real-world machine learning problems.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors deliberately stop at the basic workflow (Sequential model, compile, fit, evaluate, predict). More advanced APIs (the Functional API, subclassing, callbacks, custom training steps) are left for chapter 7.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets expectations: you do not need to understand every Keras feature before training useful models. Chapter 4 uses exactly the tools listed in the summary.
connections: p.84: the chapter opener promised you would be ready for practical applications starting with chapter 4.
p.254: chapter 7's summary lists the fuller spectrum of Keras workflows.

paragraphs.excerpt: TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX are three popular low-level frameworks for
paragraphs.what_it_says: TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are low-level frameworks for numerical computation and autodifferentiation, each with its own approach, strengths and weaknesses.
paragraphs.what_it_means: All three provide tensors, tensor operations and automatic gradients, the three low-level ingredients listed on p.87. They differ in style: TensorFlow with tf.function compilation and tf.GradientTape, PyTorch with eager modules and loss.backward(), JAX with pure functions, explicit state and jax.grad / jax.jit.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Understanding that they offer the same core capabilities explains why Keras can sit on top of any of them.

terminology.meaning: Automatic computation of gradients of programs built from differentiable operations.

connections: p.87: how the frameworks relate to each other (Keras as the prefabricated kit, the others as raw materials).
p.98, p.105, p.114: the 'What makes the ... approach unique' subsections for each framework.

paragraphs.excerpt: Keras is a high-level API for building and training neural networks.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Keras is a high-level API for neural networks that runs on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX; you choose the backend.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Keras code is written once against Keras APIs; the backend is selected by configuration (the KERAS_BACKEND environment variable or the Keras config file), with 'tensorflow', 'torch' or 'jax'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: You are not locked into one ecosystem: the book notes you could debug in PyTorch, train on TPU with JAX, and serve with TensorFlow tooling (p.115). All later Keras examples in the book run on all three.
connections: p.115: picking a backend framework; TensorFlow is the default backend.
p.116: use the string "torch" (not "pytorch"); the authors recommend JAX if you have no preference.

paragraphs.excerpt: The central class of Keras is the Layer. A layer encapsulates
paragraphs.what_it_says: Layer is Keras's central class; a layer holds weights and computation, and layers are assembled into models.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A layer = state (weights created in build()) + a forward computation (call()). A model is a graph of layers, e.g. Sequential stacks them linearly.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the unit of abstraction used throughout the book; every architecture (convnets, RNNs, Transformers) is built from layers.
connections: p.116: Layers: the building blocks of deep learning.

paragraphs.excerpt: Before you start training a model, you need to pick an
paragraphs.what_it_says: Before training you pick an optimizer, a loss and metrics and pass them to model.compile().
paragraphs.what_it_means: The loss is what gradient descent minimises; the optimizer decides how gradients become weight updates; metrics are what you monitor and need not be differentiable (p.122).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Choosing the wrong loss for the task (e.g. MSE for multiclass classification) is one of the most common beginner errors; section 3.6.5 gives guidance.

paragraphs.excerpt: To train a model, you can use the fit() method, which
paragraphs.what_it_says: fit() runs mini-batch gradient descent for you and can also monitor loss and metrics on validation data, inputs the model does not see during training.
paragraphs.what_it_means: fit() hides the training loop you wrote by hand in sections 3.3.2, 3.4.2 and 3.5.4: batching, forward pass, gradient computation, optimizer step, metric tracking. validation_data adds an evaluation pass at the end of each epoch.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It lets you focus on model and data rather than loop mechanics; the validation numbers it reports are how you detect overfitting (chapter 5).
connections: p.125-126: monitoring on validation data, and keeping it strictly separate.

paragraphs.excerpt: Once your model is trained, you can use the model.predict() method
paragraphs.what_it_says: After training, model.predict() generates predictions on new inputs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: predict() runs batched inference and returns a NumPy array, exactly as the output at the top of this page illustrates.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Inference is the end goal of training; chapter 4 uses predict() for each of its three examples.
connections: p.126: predict() versus calling the model directly.

concepts.name: model.predict() output
concepts.definition: A NumPy array whose first axis indexes samples; for a Dense(1) model, shape (N, 1).
concepts.intuition: One row per input, one column per output unit.
concepts.technical: The printed block is predictions[:10], a (10, 1) float32 array. Each value is w·x + b for one validation point.
concepts.significance: Shows concretely what inference returns, and that turning scores into decisions is a separate step.
concepts.misconception: "The values are probabilities." They are unconstrained linear outputs; they just happen to lie in [0, 1] here because the model was trained toward 0/1 targets.

concepts.name: Keras backends
concepts.definition: The low-level framework (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX) that executes Keras's tensor operations and gradients.
concepts.intuition: Keras is the steering wheel; the backend is the engine you can swap.
concepts.technical: Selected before importing Keras; Keras layers, losses and optimizers dispatch to backend ops through keras.ops.
concepts.significance: Write once, run on any backend; choose per task (debugging, TPU training, deployment).
concepts.misconception: "Keras is part of TensorFlow only." Keras 3 is multi-backend.

concepts.name: Layer
concepts.definition: The central Keras class: encapsulates weights and computation.
concepts.intuition: A reusable building block that transforms tensors and remembers what it learned.
concepts.technical: Weights are created in build() (possibly lazily, on first call) and the computation lives in call().
concepts.significance: Every model in the book is assembled from layers.
concepts.misconception: "A layer is just a function." It also owns state (weights).

concepts.name: The basic Keras workflow
concepts.definition: Build a model from layers -> compile(optimizer, loss, metrics) -> fit(data, validation_data) -> predict(new data).
concepts.technical: compile() configures; fit() runs mini-batch gradient descent; evaluate() and predict() run forward passes only.
concepts.significance: The recipe used for every example in chapter 4.
concepts.example: Listing 3.35 plus the predict() call on p.126.
concepts.misconception: "fit() is the only way to train." Chapter 7 shows custom train_step() and fully custom loops.

code.title: Output of print(predictions[:10])
code.what_it_does: This is not code but the console output of the two lines at the bottom of p.126 (`predictions = model.predict(val_inputs, batch_size=128)` and `print(predictions[:10])`). It shows the first ten scores of the linear classifier.

line_explanations.explanation: Outer [ opens the (10, 1) array; first sample's score 0.359: below 0.5.
Scores 0.0258 and 0.166: clearly on the 'class 0' side.
Score 0.721 (above 0.5); the final ]] closes the array.

code.inputs_outputs: Input (on p.126): val_inputs. Output: a NumPy array of shape (10, 1).
code.algorithm: Each value is the linear function w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b applied to one 2-D validation point.
code.theory_link: Because the model was trained with MSE toward targets 0 and 1, the score estimates the target; BinaryAccuracy thresholds it at 0.5.
pitfalls: Values are random-seed dependent; your numbers will differ.
The trailing spaces inside brackets are just NumPy's column alignment.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written illustration (not from the book)
import numpy as np
preds = np.array([0.3590725, 0.82706255, 0.74428225, 0.682058, 0.7312616,
                  0.6059811, 0.78046083, 0.025846, 0.16594526, 0.72068727])
labels = (preds > 0.5).astype(int)
print(labels)  # [0 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 1]

deeper.title: Thresholding the printed scores
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: with the 0.5 threshold that `BinaryAccuracy` uses by default, the ten printed scores become the labels

`[0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1]`

that is, 7 samples are assigned to class 1 and 3 to class 0. Scores such as 0.606 or 0.682 are less 'confident' than 0.026 or 0.827 only in the sense that they lie nearer the decision boundary $w\cdot x + b = 0.5$; they are not calibrated probabilities. To know whether these labels are right you would compare them with `val_targets[:10]`, which the book does not print.

deeper.title: Chapter 3 at a glance
deeper.body:
- **Low level (3.3-3.5):** the same linear classifier written three times, in pure TensorFlow, pure PyTorch and pure JAX: tensors, variables/state, gradients, manual update loop.
- **High level (3.6):** the same classifier in a few lines of Keras: `Sequential([Dense(1)])`, `compile`, `fit`, `evaluate`, `predict`.

The contrast is the lesson: Keras packages the loop you wrote by hand, and runs it on whichever of the three engines you choose. (This framing is an inference from the chapter's structure.)

deeper.title: Kit vs raw materials
deeper.body: The book itself (p.87) compares Keras to a prefabricated building kit and the low-level frameworks to raw construction materials. The summary's first two bullets restate that picture: three suppliers of raw materials, one kit that works with any of them.

misconceptions.claim: The printed values are class probabilities.
misconceptions.correction: They are raw outputs of a linear Dense(1) layer without activation; they are scores, not calibrated probabilities.

misconceptions.claim: Keras is a separate alternative to TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
misconceptions.correction: Keras is a high-level API that runs on top of any one of them (summary bullet 2).

misconceptions.claim: Metrics passed to compile() are optimised during training.
misconceptions.correction: Only the loss is optimised; metrics are monitored (p.122).

takeaways: predict() on the linear model returns a (N, 1) NumPy array of scalar scores; thresholding at 0.5 turns them into class labels.
TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are low-level frameworks for tensor computation and autodiff.
Keras is a high-level API that runs on any of the three backends.
Layers (weights + computation) are assembled into models.
compile() sets optimizer, loss and metrics; fit() trains with mini-batch gradient descent and monitors validation data; predict() does inference.
You now have the tools needed for the real-world problems of chapter 4.

questions.question: What is the shape of the array printed at the top of the page?
questions.explanation: The printout has ten rows each wrapped in its own brackets, the signature of a 2-D array with one column: Dense(1) outputs one unit per sample and predictions[:10] keeps the first ten rows. (10,) would print as a flat list; (1, 10) as one row; (10, 2) would show two values per row.

questions.question: Using a 0.5 threshold, how many of the ten printed samples are predicted as class 1?
According to the summary, which statement about Keras is correct?
options: Keras is a low-level framework for autodifferentiation.
Keras is a high-level API that can run on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX.
Keras replaces the need for optimizers and losses.
questions.answer: Keras is a high-level API that can run on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX.
questions.explanation: Bullet 2 says exactly this. Bullet 1 assigns the low-level role to TF/PyTorch/JAX; Keras is multi-backend; and bullet 4 says you must still pick an optimizer and loss.

questions.question: Why can the same Keras model run on three different frameworks?
questions.answer: Because all three provide the same low-level primitives Keras needs (tensors, tensor operations, automatic differentiation), and Keras expresses layers, losses and optimizers in terms of those primitives, dispatching to whichever backend is configured.
questions.explanation: Bullet 1 identifies the shared role of the frameworks; p.87 lists the low-level ingredients each provides.

questions.question: Which method covered on p.126 is missing from the six summary bullets, and what does it do?
questions.answer: evaluate(): it computes loss and metrics on a labeled dataset (e.g. validation data) in batches after training.
questions.explanation: The summary mentions compile, fit and predict but not evaluate, which p.126 introduced.

questions.question: fit() 'runs mini-batch gradient descent for you'. Which steps from the hand-written loops of sections 3.3-3.5 does it take over?
questions.answer: Shuffling/batching the data, the forward pass, loss computation, gradient computation via the backend's autodiff, applying the optimizer update, tracking metrics, repeating over epochs, and optionally evaluating on validation data.
questions.explanation: The pure TensorFlow/PyTorch/JAX classifiers (p.93, p.102, p.112) implemented these steps manually.

questions.question: Without looking, write the six summary bullets in your own words and name the subsection where each was taught.
questions.answer: Low-level frameworks (3.3-3.5); Keras multi-backend API (3.6/3.6.1); Layer and models (3.6.2-3.6.3); compile with optimizer/loss/metrics (3.6.4-3.6.5); fit and validation (3.6.6-3.6.7); predict (3.6.8).
questions.explanation: Mapping each point back to its section consolidates the chapter.
